title: What will AI mean for humanity?
summary: A Harvard panel discussion explored how AI and digital technology are reshaping human cognition and social experience, drawing on neuroscience research showing that ChatGPT users demonstrate reduced brain engagement and ownership over their work compared to those using traditional research methods. Panelists offered contrasting perspectives: some warned that AI tools undermine the cognitive struggle necessary for learning and fulfillment, while others argued that technology can be redesigned to cultivate reverence and shared understanding rather than domination. The conversation situated contemporary AI concerns within longer intellectual traditions questioning technology's role in work, agency, creativity, and what constitutes essential versus instrumental human activity.
central_argument: Generative AI currently diminishes human cognitive engagement and ownership, but technology can be intentionally redesigned to promote spiritual intelligence, shared meaning-making, and reverence rather than domination.
key_claims: ChatGPT users showed significantly less brain activity during essay writing than those using internet search or their own intelligence alone
83% of ChatGPT users could not quote their own essays one minute after submission, compared to 11% in control groups
Brain development requires struggle; tasks that are too easy prevent cognitive bloom and learning
Current social media technology is engineered around commercial advertising rather than community awareness and shared experience
More than 80% of scientists report encountering deep respect and reverence for what they study, suggesting science differs fundamentally from technology in its underlying orientation
Large language models can prompt education to rethink what is instrumental versus essential human activity
key_tensions: The article argues against the assumption that technology's only viable business model is advertising-based, citing Weyl's claim this constraint is not structural but chosen
It complicates the notion that technology inevitably produces domination and extraction, countering with evidence that scientific practice operates from reverence and receptivity
It pushes back on treating all cognitive labor as equally valuable, arguing that struggle and difficulty are necessary preconditions for learning and ownership
key_entities: Nataliya Kos'myna (MIT Media Lab brain activity study)
Steven Pinker (When Everyone Knows That Everyone Knows)
